tagline: Rice country and coastal marsh meet an old beach of shells.
intro: At Hayes, Louisiana Highway 14 runs through town beside Bayou Lacassine; farther east, it connects Gueydan, Kaplan and Abbeville. Gueydan’s rice country occupies nearly flat prairie. In Abbeville, the Vermilion River passes through downtown. Pecan Island occupies a different kind of ground: prehistoric beach ridges surrounded by coastal marsh.

A road-building effort linked the prairie towns in the 1920s. The Lafitte Cut-Off Old Spanish Trail project began in 1923, planned between New Iberia and Lake Charles by way of Abbeville, Kaplan, Gueydan, Lake Arthur and Hayes. J. W. Gardiner represented Hayes on its elected committee. By July 1925, only three miles on each side of Bayou Lacassine remained unfinished.

From Hayes, LA 14 leads south and east toward Lake Arthur. Farther east, Gueydan and Kaplan lead toward Abbeville along LA 14. Pecan Island lies south of White Lake’s southeastern corner, on an old Gulf beach made of crushed shells and sand.

moments.title: Hayes
moments.text: In 1905, Bill Cox put the Methodist church on a logging wagon and moved it into Hayes. The railroad had changed where people lived, and the congregation considered its old location out of the way. The Louisiana Western Railroad had completed its line through Hayes in 1904. Toliver Hayes sold the company a right-of-way, a depot site and 40 acres for a town site. The community stands on Bayou Lacassine’s west bank, where the water forms the parish boundary. The church had begun in 1898 as a single room with a small foot-operated organ.

moments.title: Gueydan
moments.text: Surveyors dismissed the land the Gueydan brothers bought in 1884 as “sea marsh, unfit for cultivation.” An irrigation pump at nearby Primeaux Landing helped the area grow as a rice producer, supplying water to thousands of acres. Jean Pierre Gueydan also donated land and right-of-way to induce the Southern Pacific Railroad to build a branch from Midland. Drainage canals and rice development reduced the wetlands’ capacity to absorb floods; in August 1940, flooding inundated the entire town. The surrounding, nearly flat prairie averages only nine feet above the Gulf of Mexico.

moments.title: Pecan Island
moments.text: Front Ridge and Back Ridge meet beneath Pecan Island. They are cheniers, prehistoric beach ridges surrounded by coastal marsh. Front Ridge runs west to east, with other ridges branching northeast from it. Its shelly fine sand lies over muddy brackish and salt-marsh deposits. The ridge reaches a maximum elevation of about seven feet above sea level. Back Ridge’s sand and shell fragments instead lie over shallow marine or mudflat sediments. The community lies directly south of White Lake’s southeastern corner. Most residents are of Cajun ancestry, and the community holds Mardi Gras.
moments.notice: The community occupies the junction of two old beach ridges amid coastal marsh.
